question: What is the form of government of the United States?
explanation: In the United States the people are not ruled by a king or queen. They govern themselves by electing representatives to serve in local, state and national government, which is what a republic or representative democracy means. (Study guide, chapter 1.)

question: What is the supreme law of the land?
explanation: The Constitution says of itself that it is the supreme law of the land. Everyone living in the United States, and every level of government, must follow it. (Study guide, chapter 1.)

question: Name one thing the U.S. Constitution does.
correct_answers: Protects the rights of the people
explanation: The Constitution, written in 1787, sets up the government and protects the basic rights of the people. Its first three sections describe the three branches and the powers each one has. (Study guide, chapter 1.)

question: The U.S. Constitution starts with the words “We the People.” What does “We the People” mean?
explanation: These first three words of the Constitution carry the idea of self-government. The people of the United States are not governed by a king or queen: they govern themselves by electing representatives. (Study guide, chapter 1.)

question: How are changes made to the U.S. Constitution?
explanation: A change to the Constitution is called an amendment. An amendment is added only when three-fourths of the states approve it, which today means 38 of the 50. (Study guide, chapter 1.)

question: What does the Bill of Rights protect?
correct_answers: (The basic) rights of people living in the United States
explanation: The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments to the Constitution, added in 1791. It lists some of the basic rights of people living in the United States, such as freedom of speech and religion. (Study guide, chapter 1.)

question: How many amendments does the U.S. Constitution have?
explanation: There have been 27 changes, called amendments, since the Constitution was written. The first ten are the Bill of Rights, and later ones cover matters such as who can be a citizen and who can vote. (Study guide, chapter 1.)

question: Why is the Declaration of Independence important?
correct_answers: It says America is free from British control.
It says all people are created equal.
explanation: The Declaration of Independence, adopted on July 4, 1776, announced that the colonies were free from Great Britain. In it Thomas Jefferson wrote that everyone has the right to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. (Study guide, chapter 8.)

source.title: 128 Civics Questions and Answers (2025 version)
source.quote_under_25_words: It says America is free from British control.

question: What founding document said the American colonies were free from Britain?
explanation: The Declaration of Independence announced independence from Great Britain when it was adopted on July 4, 1776. The study guide calls it a statement of freedom. (Study guide, chapter 8.)

question: Name two important ideas from the Declaration of Independence and the U.S. Constitution.
explanation: You need to name two. The guide teaches that the Declaration speaks of the right to liberty, and that both documents rest on self-government: the people govern themselves. (Study guide, chapter 8.)

question: The words “Life, Liberty, and the pursuit of Happiness” are in what founding document?
explanation: Thomas Jefferson wrote in the Declaration of Independence that everyone has the right to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. The words are not from the Constitution, which was written eleven years later. (Study guide, chapter 8.)

question: What is the economic system of the United States?
explanation: The economic system of the United States is called a capitalist or market economy. In it the government does not control the economy, and people are free to start a business and make money. (Study guide, chapter 11.)

question: What is the rule of law?
correct_answers: No one is above the law.
explanation: The rule of law means that no one is above the law and everyone must follow it. That includes the President and the federal, state and local governments. (Study guide, chapter 1.)

question: Many documents influenced the U.S. Constitution. Name one.
explanation: You need to name one document from the official list. The study guide covers two of them: the Declaration of Independence of 1776, and the Federalist Papers, written to support passing the Constitution. (Study guide, chapter 5.)

question: There are three branches of government. Why?
correct_answers: So one part does not become too powerful
explanation: The Founders feared that one person or group with too much power could take over the country. They gave each branch different powers, called the separation of powers, so that no branch becomes too powerful. (Study guide, chapter 1.)

source.title: 128 Civics Questions and Answers (2025 version)
source.quote_under_25_words: So one part does not become too powerful

question: Name the three branches of government.
explanation: The first three sections of the Constitution set up the legislative branch (Congress), the executive branch (led by the President) and the judicial branch (the Supreme Court and other federal courts). Either way of naming all three is accepted. (Study guide, chapter 1.)

question: The President of the United States is in charge of which branch of government?
explanation: The President of the United States is in charge of the executive branch, which enforces federal laws. The Vice President, the Cabinet and the federal departments and agencies are part of it too. (Study guide, chapter 3.)

question: What part of the federal government writes laws?
explanation: The Constitution says that Congress makes federal laws. Congress is the legislative branch, and the Founders described it in the first section of the Constitution because they thought making laws the most important power. (Study guide, chapter 2.)

question: What are the two parts of the U.S. Congress?
explanation: Congress has two parts, the Senate and the House of Representatives. The Founders agreed on two so that larger states have more members in the House while every state has two senators. (Study guide, chapter 2.)

question: Name one power of the U.S. Congress.
explanation: Congress writes the federal laws. It also votes to declare war, as it did the day after Pearl Harbor was attacked in 1941. (Study guide, chapter 2.)

question: How many U.S. senators are there?
explanation: Each of the 50 states has two senators, which makes 100. Senators represent all the people of their state. (Study guide, chapter 2.)

question: How long is a term for a U.S. senator?
explanation: Senators are elected for six years. That is three times as long as the two-year term of a member of the House of Representatives. (Study guide, chapter 2.)

question: Who is one of your state’s U.S. senators now?
correct_answers: Answers will vary. [District of Columbia residents and residents of U.S. territories should answer that D.C. (or the territory where the applicant lives) has no U.S. senators.]
explanation: The answer depends on where you live, so look up your state's two senators at senate.gov before the interview. Washington, D.C., is not a state and has no senators, and residents there should say so. (Study guide, chapter 2.)

question: How many voting members are in the House of Representatives?
explanation: The House has 435 voting members, each elected from a congressional district. States with more people have more districts, and so more members. (Study guide, chapter 2.)

question: How long is a term for a member of the House of Representatives?
explanation: Members of the House of Representatives are elected every two years. Senators, by contrast, serve six years. (Study guide, chapter 2.)

question: Why do U.S. representatives serve shorter terms than U.S. senators?
correct_answers: To more closely follow public opinion
explanation: The official answer is that a shorter term keeps representatives closer to public opinion. The study guide gives the terms, two years for the House and six for the Senate, but not this reason. (From the official list of answers.)

question: How many senators does each state have?
explanation: Every state has two senators, however many people live there. California, the largest state, and Wyoming, the smallest, both have two. (Study guide, chapter 2.)

question: Why does each state have two senators?
explanation: At the Constitutional Convention the Founders disagreed about how many representatives each state should have. They settled on a Congress with two parts: seats in the House follow population, and every state gets the same two seats in the Senate. (Study guide, chapter 2.)

question: Name your U.S. representative.
correct_answers: Answers will vary. [Residents of territories with nonvoting Delegates or Resident Commissioners may provide the name of that Delegate or Commissioner. Also acceptable is any statement that the territory has no (voting) representatives in Congress.]
explanation: The answer depends on your congressional district, so look up your representative at house.gov before the interview. Residents of a territory may name their delegate, or say the territory has no voting representative. (Study guide, chapter 2.)

explanation: The Speaker leads the House of Representatives, and the name changes when the House chooses a new one. Check uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates or speaker.gov for the Speaker serving at the time of your interview. (Study guide, chapter 2.)

question: Who does a U.S. senator represent?
explanation: A senator represents all the people of a state, not one district within it. Every state has two. (Study guide, chapter 2.)

question: Who elects U.S. senators?
explanation: Senators are chosen by the voters of their own state. They are elected for six years and must live in the state they represent. (Study guide, chapter 2.)

question: Who does a member of the House of Representatives represent?
explanation: Each state is divided into congressional districts, and each district elects one member of the House. That member represents the people of the district. (Study guide, chapter 2.)

question: Who elects members of the House of Representatives?
explanation: The voters of each congressional district elect that district's member of the House. Elections for the House are held every two years. (Study guide, chapter 2.)

question: Some states have more representatives than other states. Why?
explanation: Seats in the House depend on how many people live in a state. California, with the most people, has 52 voting members, and Wyoming, with the fewest, has one. (Study guide, chapter 2.)

question: The President of the United States is elected for how many years?
explanation: Citizens vote for President in November, and the President is elected for four years. A person can be elected President only twice. (Study guide, chapter 3.)

question: The President of the United States can serve only two terms. Why?
correct_answers: To keep the president from becoming too powerful
explanation: The 22nd Amendment, added in 1951, says a person can be elected President only two times. It followed Franklin Roosevelt, who was elected four times. (Study guide, chapter 11.)

question: What is the name of the President of the United States now?
correct_answers: Visit uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for the name of the President of the United States.
explanation: The answer is whoever holds the office at the time of your interview, so it changes after an election. Check uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates or whitehouse.gov shortly before you go. (Study guide, chapter 3.)

source.title: 128 Civics Questions and Answers (2025 version)

question: What is the name of the Vice President of the United States now?
correct_answers: Visit uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for the name of the Vice President of the United States.
explanation: The answer is whoever is Vice President at the time of your interview. Check uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates or whitehouse.gov shortly before you go. (Study guide, chapter 3.)

source.title: 128 Civics Questions and Answers (2025 version)
source.quote_under_25_words: Visit uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for the name of the Vice President of the United States.

question: If the president can no longer serve, who becomes president?
correct_answers: The Vice President (of the United States)
explanation: The Constitution says that if the President can no longer serve, the Vice President becomes President. This has happened when Presidents died in office. (Study guide, chapter 3.)

source.title: 128 Civics Questions and Answers (2025 version)
source.quote_under_25_words: The Vice President (of the United States)

question: Name one power of the president.
explanation: The President signs bills into law or vetoes them, and enforces the laws as head of the executive branch. The President is also Commander in Chief of the military. (Study guide, chapter 3.)

question: Who is Commander in Chief of the U.S. military?
explanation: The President is the Commander in Chief, in charge of everyone serving in the U.S. Armed Forces. Serving in the Armed Forces is voluntary. (Study guide, chapter 3.)

question: Who signs bills to become laws?
explanation: When both parts of Congress pass a bill, it goes to the President. If the President agrees, the President signs it and it becomes a law everyone must follow. (Study guide, chapter 2.)

question: Who vetoes bills?
explanation: If the President does not agree with a bill, the President vetoes it, which means not signing it. The bill then does not become law unless Congress votes to override the veto. (Study guide, chapter 2.)

question: Who appoints federal judges?
explanation: The President nominates people to be federal judges, including Supreme Court justices. The Senate must then approve them, so more than one branch is involved. (Study guide, chapter 4.)

question: The executive branch has many parts. Name one.
explanation: The executive branch is led by the President. It also includes the Vice President, the President's Cabinet, and the federal departments and agencies. (Study guide, chapter 3.)

question: What does the President’s Cabinet do?
correct_answers: Advises the President (of the United States)
explanation: A cabinet is a group of advisors, and the President's Cabinet advises the President. Its members lead the executive departments. (Study guide, chapter 3.)

source.title: 128 Civics Questions and Answers (2025 version)
source.quote_under_25_words: Advises the President (of the United States)

question: What are two Cabinet-level positions?
correct_answers: Secretary of Health and Human Services
Secretary of Housing and Urban Development
Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency
Administrator of the Small Business Administration
Director of the Central Intelligence Agency
Director of the Office of Management and Budget
explanation: You need to name two. Most Cabinet members are called Secretary, such as the Secretary of State or the Secretary of Homeland Security, while the head of the Department of Justice is the Attorney General. (Study guide, chapter 3.)

question: Why is the Electoral College important?
correct_answers: It decides who is elected president.
It provides a compromise between the popular election of the president and congressional selection.
explanation: The official list gives two answers: it decides who is elected President, and it is a compromise between a popular election and selection by Congress. The study guide's chapters do not describe the Electoral College. (From the official list of answers.)

source.title: 128 Civics Questions and Answers (2025 version)

question: What is one part of the judicial branch?
explanation: The judicial branch is made up of the Supreme Court and the other federal courts. The Supreme Court is the highest of them. (Study guide, chapter 4.)

question: What does the judicial branch do?
correct_answers: Decides if a law goes against the (U.S.) Constitution
explanation: The judicial branch reviews laws and can decide whether a law follows the Constitution. It can do so only when a legal case is brought before a court. (Study guide, chapter 4.)

question: What is the highest court in the United States?
explanation: The Supreme Court is the highest court in the United States, so its decision about a law or a case is final. No other court can change it. (Study guide, chapter 4.)

question: How many seats are on the Supreme Court?
explanation: There are nine justices on the Supreme Court. One of them is the Chief Justice of the United States. (Study guide, chapter 4.)

question: How many Supreme Court justices are usually needed to decide a case?
explanation: A decision needs a majority, which means more than half of the justices. When all nine hear a case, at least five must vote the same way. (Study guide, chapter 4.)

question: How long do Supreme Court justices serve?
explanation: The official answer is that justices serve for life, or until they retire. The study guide explains that they are appointed, not elected, but does not state the length of their service. (From the official list of answers.)

question: Supreme Court justices serve for life. Why?
explanation: The Founders did not want federal judges to decide cases based on politics or elections. They wanted decisions based on the Constitution and the rule of law, which is why judges are not elected. (Study guide, chapter 4.)

question: Who is the Chief Justice of the United States now?
correct_answers: Visit uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for the name of the Chief Justice of the United States.
explanation: The Chief Justice leads the Supreme Court, and the name changes only when a new one is appointed. Check uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates or supremecourt.gov for the Chief Justice at the time of your interview. (Study guide, chapter 4.)

source.title: 128 Civics Questions and Answers (2025 version)
source.quote_under_25_words: Visit uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for the name of the Chief Justice of the United States.

question: Name one power that is only for the federal government.
explanation: The Constitution gives some powers to the federal government alone. Examples in the study guide are printing money, creating an army, declaring war and making treaties with other countries. (Study guide, chapter 1.)

question: Name one power that is only for the states.
explanation: Powers the Constitution does not give to the federal government belong to the states or the people. The study guide's examples are schooling, police protection and fire departments. (Study guide, chapter 1.)

question: What is the purpose of the 10th Amendment?
correct_answers: (It states that the) powers not given to the federal government belong to the states or to the people.
explanation: Powers that the Constitution neither gives to the federal government nor forbids to the states are reserved for the states or the people. That is how states come to run their own schools and police. (Study guide, chapter 1.)

source.title: 128 Civics Questions and Answers (2025 version)

explanation: Every state has its own capital city, so the answer depends on where you live. Washington, D.C., is not a state and has no capital, and residents there should say so. (Study guide, chapter 6.)

question: There are four amendments to the U.S. Constitution about who can vote. Describe one of them.
correct_answers: You don’t have to pay (a poll tax) to vote.
Any citizen can vote. (Women and men can vote.)
A male citizen of any race (can vote).
explanation: You need to describe one. The four amendments say that citizens 18 and older can vote, that nobody has to pay a poll tax to vote, that women as well as men can vote, and that a male citizen of any race can vote. (Study guide, chapter 5.)

question: Who can vote in federal elections, run for federal office, and serve on a jury in the United States?
explanation: These are rights and responsibilities of U.S. citizens only. Voting in federal elections and running for federal office are both reserved for citizens. (Study guide, chapter 5.)

question: What are three rights of everyone living in the United States?
explanation: You need to name three. The First Amendment lists five freedoms that belong to everyone living in the United States: speech, religion, assembly, the press, and petitioning the government. (Study guide, chapter 5.)

question: What do we show loyalty to when we say the Pledge of Allegiance?
explanation: Saying the Pledge of Allegiance shows loyalty to the flag and to the United States. People stand, face the flag and put their right hand over their heart. (Study guide, chapter 12.)

question: Name two promises that new citizens make in the Oath of Allegiance.
correct_answers: Give up loyalty to other countries
Obey the laws of the United States
Serve (help, do important work for) the nation (if needed)
Be loyal to the United States
explanation: You need to name two. New citizens promise to give up loyalty to other countries, to defend the Constitution and obey the laws, to serve the nation or its military if needed, and to be loyal to the United States. (Study guide, chapter 5.)

source.title: 128 Civics Questions and Answers (2025 version)
source.quote_under_25_words: Give up loyalty to other countries

question: How can people become United States citizens?
correct_answers: Be born in the United States, under the conditions set by the 14th Amendment
Derive citizenship (under conditions set by Congress)
explanation: There are three ways. A person can be born in the United States under the conditions of the 14th Amendment, can naturalize, or can derive citizenship under conditions set by Congress. (Study guide, chapter 5.)

source.title: 128 Civics Questions and Answers (2025 version)
source.quote_under_25_words: Be born in the United States, under the conditions set by the 14th Amendment

question: What are two examples of civic participation in the United States?
correct_answers: Give an elected official your opinion (on an issue)
Support or oppose an issue or policy
explanation: You need to name two. The study guide gives examples such as voting, writing to a newspaper, and publicly giving an opinion about an issue or policy. (Study guide, chapter 5.)

question: What is one way Americans can serve their country?
correct_answers: Work for local, state, or federal government
explanation: Obeying the law and paying taxes are responsibilities of everyone living in the United States. Citizens can also serve by voting, and serving in the Armed Forces is voluntary. (Study guide, chapter 5.)

question: Why is it important to pay federal taxes?
correct_answers: All people pay to fund the federal government
explanation: The law requires everyone living in the United States to pay federal income tax. People send in a federal income tax form each year, and the last day to do so is April 15. (Study guide, chapter 5.)

question: It is important for all men age 18 through 25 to register for the Selective Service. Name one reason why.
correct_answers: Makes the draft fair, if needed
explanation: Registering is required by law for men who are citizens or legal residents. The official list also accepts that it is a civic duty and that it makes a draft fair if one is ever needed. (Study guide, chapter 5.)

question: The colonists came to America for many reasons. Name one.
explanation: Many colonists who settled at Jamestown came for economic opportunity, such as land to farm. Others, like the Pilgrims who founded Massachusetts in 1620, came for religious freedom. (Study guide, chapter 7.)

question: Who lived in America before the Europeans arrived?
explanation: Native Americans, also called American Indians, lived in the Americas for around 20,000 years before Europeans arrived. There were many tribes, each with its own culture, language and form of government. (Study guide, chapter 7.)

question: What group of people was taken and sold as slaves?
explanation: Millions of people were taken from Africa by force and sold as slaves in North and South America. The first group of enslaved Africans was brought to Jamestown in 1619. (Study guide, chapter 7.)

question: What war did the Americans fight to win independence from Britain?
explanation: The colonists went to war with Great Britain in 1775, in what is called the American Revolutionary War. It ended in 1783, when Britain signed a treaty agreeing that the United States was independent. (Study guide, chapter 8.)

question: Name one reason why the Americans declared independence from Britain.
correct_answers: British soldiers stayed in Americans’ houses (boarding, quartering)
explanation: Britain raised taxes on the colonies without letting their representatives vote, which the colonists called taxation without representation. It then made the colonial congresses illegal, leaving the colonists without self-government. (Study guide, chapter 8.)

question: Who wrote the Declaration of Independence?
explanation: Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration of Independence. In it he wrote that everyone has the right to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. (Study guide, chapter 8.)

question: When was the Declaration of Independence adopted?
explanation: The Declaration of Independence was adopted on July 4, 1776. That is why Independence Day is celebrated on July 4. (Study guide, chapter 8.)

question: The American Revolution had many important events. Name one.
correct_answers: Washington Crossing the Delaware (Battle of Trenton)
explanation: You need to name one event from the official list. The study guide covers two of them: the adoption of the Declaration of Independence in 1776, and the British surrender at Yorktown, Virginia, in 1781. (Study guide, chapter 8.)

question: There were 13 original states. Name five.
explanation: You need to name five. When the colonists adopted the Declaration of Independence, the 13 colonies along the East Coast became the 13 original states, from New Hampshire in the north to Georgia in the south. (Study guide, chapter 8.)

question: What founding document was written in 1787?
explanation: The Constitution was written in 1787 at the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia. That was eleven years after the Declaration of Independence. (Study guide, chapter 1.)

question: The Federalist Papers supported the passage of the U.S. Constitution. Name one of the writers.
explanation: James Madison, Alexander Hamilton and John Jay wrote the Federalist Papers. They signed all of the essays with the name Publius, which is why that name is accepted too. (Study guide, chapter 5.)

question: Why were the Federalist Papers important?
correct_answers: They helped people understand the (U.S.) Constitution.
explanation: The Federalist Papers were 85 essays printed in newspapers in 1787 and 1788. They supported passing the Constitution at a time when many people did not like it. (Study guide, chapter 5.)

source.title: 128 Civics Questions and Answers (2025 version)
source.quote_under_25_words: They helped people understand the (U.S.) Constitution.

question: Benjamin Franklin is famous for many things. Name one.
correct_answers: Founded the first free public libraries
First Postmaster General of the United States
Helped write the Declaration of Independence
explanation: Benjamin Franklin was a diplomat who negotiated the treaty with Great Britain in 1783. The official list also accepts that he was the first Postmaster General, started the first free libraries, and was an inventor. (Study guide, chapter 8.)

source.title: 128 Civics Questions and Answers (2025 version)
source.quote_under_25_words: Founded the first free public libraries

question: George Washington is famous for many things. Name one.
correct_answers: First president of the United States
explanation: George Washington was the general of the colonial army in the Revolutionary War and then the first President, serving from 1789 to 1797. He is known as the Father of Our Country. (Study guide, chapter 9.)

question: Thomas Jefferson is famous for many things. Name one.
correct_answers: Writer of the Declaration of Independence
Third president of the United States
Doubled the size of the United States (Louisiana Purchase)
Writer of the Virginia Statute on Religious Freedom
explanation: Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration of Independence. The official list accepts other answers the study guide does not teach, such as his being the third President. (Study guide, chapter 8.)

source.title: 128 Civics Questions and Answers (2025 version)
source.quote_under_25_words: Writer of the Declaration of Independence

question: James Madison is famous for many things. Name one.
correct_answers: Fourth president of the United States
One of the writers of the Federalist Papers
explanation: James Madison was one of the Founders at the Constitutional Convention and one of the three writers of the Federalist Papers. The official list also accepts that he was the fourth President. (Study guide, chapter 5.)

question: Alexander Hamilton is famous for many things. Name one.
correct_answers: One of the writers of the Federalist Papers
Helped establish the First Bank of the United States
explanation: Alexander Hamilton was one of the three writers of the Federalist Papers, with James Madison and John Jay. The official list also accepts that he was the first Secretary of the Treasury. (Study guide, chapter 5.)

question: What territory did the United States buy from France in 1803?
explanation: In 1803 the United States bought the Louisiana Territory from France. It was a large area of land between the Mississippi River and the Rocky Mountains. (Study guide, chapter 9.)

question: Name one war fought by the United States in the 1800s.
explanation: The study guide names four wars the United States fought in the 1800s. They are the War of 1812, the Mexican-American War, the Civil War and the Spanish-American War. (Study guide, chapter 9.)

question: Name the U.S. war between the North and the South.
explanation: The Civil War was fought between the North and the South from 1861 to 1865. It began after eleven Southern states left the United States and formed the Confederate States of America. (Study guide, chapter 10.)

question: The Civil War had many important events. Name one.
explanation: You need to name one event from the official list. The study guide covers the Emancipation Proclamation, the South's surrender in April 1865, and the assassination of Abraham Lincoln a few days later. (Study guide, chapter 10.)

question: Abraham Lincoln is famous for many things. Name one.
correct_answers: Led the United States during the Civil War
explanation: Abraham Lincoln was the 16th President and led the United States during the Civil War. He signed the Emancipation Proclamation, which declared enslaved people in most Southern states free. (Study guide, chapter 10.)

question: What did the Emancipation Proclamation do?
correct_answers: Freed slaves in the Confederate states
Freed slaves in most Southern states
explanation: The Emancipation Proclamation announced that people enslaved in most Southern states were free. Most of them were not actually freed until the Civil War was over. (Study guide, chapter 10.)

question: What U.S. war ended slavery?
explanation: After the Civil War ended in 1865, all the people enslaved in the Southern states were freed. The 13th Amendment, added that December, made slavery illegal in the United States. (Study guide, chapter 10.)

question: What amendment says all persons born or naturalized in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof, are U.S. citizens?
explanation: The 14th Amendment sets the conditions under which a person born in the United States is a citizen. Being born in the United States is one of the three ways of becoming a citizen. (Study guide, chapter 5.)

question: When did all men get the right to vote?
explanation: The 15th Amendment, added in 1870, says that a male citizen of any race can vote. It came after the Civil War. (Study guide, chapter 5.)

question: Name one leader of the women’s rights movement in the 1800s.
explanation: Susan B. Anthony fought for women's rights in the 1800s, and wanted women to have the right to vote. The official list accepts five other names as well. (Study guide, chapter 10.)

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
question: Name one war fought by the United States in the 1900s.
explanation: The study guide names five wars the United States fought in the 1900s. They are World War I, World War II, the Korean War, the Vietnam War and the Persian Gulf War. (Study guide, chapter 11.)

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
question: Why did the United States enter World War I?
correct_answers: To support the Allied Powers (England, France, Italy, and Russia)
To oppose the Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, and Bulgaria)
explanation: The official list gives three accepted reasons, the first being that Germany attacked U.S. civilian ships. The study guide says only that the United States joined the war in 1917 and fought until 1918. (From the official list of answers.)

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
question: When did all women get the right to vote?
explanation: The 19th Amendment, added in 1920, says that any citizen, women as well as men, can vote. That was shortly after World War I ended in 1918. (Study guide, chapter 5.)

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
question: What was the Great Depression?
correct_answers: Longest economic recession in modern history
explanation: The Great Depression was the worst time for the U.S. economy in American history. Banks and businesses closed, and many people lost their jobs, homes and money. (Study guide, chapter 11.)

source.title: 128 Civics Questions and Answers (2025 version)
source.quote_under_25_words: Longest economic recession in modern history

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
question: When did the Great Depression start?
explanation: The official answer is the stock market crash of 1929, called the Great Crash. The study guide describes the Depression but does not give the year it began. (From the official list of answers.)

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
question: Who was president during the Great Depression and World War II?
explanation: Franklin Roosevelt was elected President in 1933, during the Great Depression, and served until he died in 1945, near the end of World War II. He was elected four times, more than any other President. (Study guide, chapter 11.)

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
question: Why did the United States enter World War II?
correct_answers: To support the Allied Powers (England, France, and Russia)
To oppose the Axis Powers (Germany, Italy, and Japan)
explanation: On December 7, 1941, Japan attacked the U.S. naval base at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii. The next day President Roosevelt announced that the United States would enter the war, and Congress voted to declare war. (Study guide, chapter 11.)

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
question: Dwight Eisenhower is famous for many things. Name one.
correct_answers: President at the end of (during) the Korean War
Signed the Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 (Created the Interstate System)
explanation: Dwight Eisenhower was a general in World War II. He became the 34th President in 1953 and served until 1961. (Study guide, chapter 11.)

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
question: Who was the United States’ main rival during the Cold War?
explanation: After World War II the United States and the Soviet Union, which was Russia and the countries it controlled, did not trust each other. Their rivalry, the Cold War, lasted until the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991. (Study guide, chapter 11.)

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
question: During the Cold War, what was one main concern of the United States?
explanation: The main concern of the United States during the Cold War was the spread of communism. Communism is a type of government in which the government plans the economy and controls most resources. (Study guide, chapter 11.)

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
question: Why did the United States enter the Korean War?
correct_answers: To stop the spread of communism
explanation: During the Cold War the United States wanted to stop other countries from becoming communist. North Korea was one of the countries the study guide names as becoming communist. (Study guide, chapter 11.)

source.title: 128 Civics Questions and Answers (2025 version)
source.quote_under_25_words: To stop the spread of communism

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
question: Why did the United States enter the Vietnam War?
correct_answers: To stop the spread of communism
explanation: During the Cold War the United States wanted to stop other countries from becoming communist. The Vietnam War was one of the wars it fought in the 1900s for that reason. (Study guide, chapter 11.)

source.title: 128 Civics Questions and Answers (2025 version)
source.quote_under_25_words: To stop the spread of communism

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
question: What did the civil rights movement do?
explanation: The civil rights movement was the movement to end racial discrimination in the United States. It led Congress to pass the Civil Rights Act in 1964 and the Voting Rights Act in 1965. (Study guide, chapter 11.)

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
question: Martin Luther King, Jr. is famous for many things. Name one.
correct_answers: Worked for equality for all Americans
Worked to ensure that people would “not be judged by the color of their skin, but by the content of their character”
explanation: Martin Luther King, Jr., was a leader of the civil rights movement who organized peaceful protests against racial discrimination. He gave his famous “I Have a Dream” speech at the Lincoln Memorial in 1963. (Study guide, chapter 11.)

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
question: Why did the United States enter the Persian Gulf War?
correct_answers: To force the Iraqi military from Kuwait
explanation: The official answer is that the United States went to war to force the Iraqi military out of Kuwait. The study guide lists the Persian Gulf War among the wars of the 1900s but does not explain it. (From the official list of answers.)

source.title: 128 Civics Questions and Answers (2025 version)
source.quote_under_25_words: To force the Iraqi military from Kuwait

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
question: What major event happened on September 11, 2001 in the United States?
correct_answers: Terrorists took over two planes and crashed them into the World Trade Center in New York City
Terrorists took over a plane and crashed into the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia
Terrorists took over a plane originally aimed at Washington, D.C., and crashed in a field in Pennsylvania
explanation: On September 11, 2001, terrorists hijacked four airplanes. Two hit the World Trade Center in New York City, one hit the Pentagon in Virginia, and one crashed in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, and almost 3,000 people died. (Study guide, chapter 11.)

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
question: Name one U.S. military conflict after the September 11, 2001 attacks.
explanation: The official list accepts three answers: the War on Terror, the war in Afghanistan and the war in Iraq. The study guide's history chapter ends with the attacks of September 11, 2001, and does not cover them. (From the official list of answers.)

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
question: Name one American Indian tribe in the United States.
correct_answers: Tuscarora For a complete list of tribes, please visit bia.gov.
explanation: Native Americans are also called American Indians, and there are over 500 tribes in the United States today. The study guide lists examples such as the Cherokee, Navajo, Sioux, Apache and Hopi. (Study guide, chapter 9.)

subtopic: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
question: Name one example of an American innovation.
explanation: You need to name one innovation from the official list. One the study guide describes is the moon landing: in 1969 the United States became the first country to land a person on the moon. (Study guide, chapter 11.)

question: What is the capital of the United States?
explanation: The capital is Washington, D.C., named after George Washington. D.C. stands for District of Columbia, and it is not part of any state. (Study guide, chapter 6.)

question: Where is the Statue of Liberty?
correct_answers: Liberty Island [Also acceptable are New Jersey, near New York City, and on the Hudson (River).]
explanation: The Statue of Liberty stands on Liberty Island in New York Harbor. France gave it to the United States in 1886 as a symbol of friendship. (Study guide, chapter 12.)

question: Why does the flag have 13 stripes?
correct_answers: (Because the stripes) represent the original colonies
explanation: The flag has 13 red and white stripes. They represent the 13 original colonies. (Study guide, chapter 12.)

question: Why does the flag have 50 stars?
correct_answers: (Because there is) one star for each state
explanation: There are 50 stars on the flag, one for each state. Hawaii became the 50th state in 1959. (Study guide, chapter 12.)

source.title: 128 Civics Questions and Answers (2025 version)
source.quote_under_25_words: (Because there is) one star for each state

question: What is the name of the national anthem?
explanation: The national anthem is “The Star-Spangled Banner”. Francis Scott Key wrote it about seeing the American flag after a battle in the War of 1812. (Study guide, chapter 12.)

question: The Nation’s first motto was “E Pluribus Unum.” What does that mean?
explanation: The official answer is “Out of many, one”, or “We all become one”. The study guide's chapter on symbols does not cover the motto. (From the official list of answers.)

question: What is Independence Day?
correct_answers: A holiday to celebrate U.S. independence (from Britain)
explanation: Independence Day, the Fourth of July, celebrates the Declaration of Independence and the birth of the nation. The Declaration was adopted on July 4, 1776. (Study guide, chapter 12.)

source.title: 128 Civics Questions and Answers (2025 version)
source.quote_under_25_words: A holiday to celebrate U.S. independence (from Britain)

question: Name three national U.S. holidays.
explanation: You need to name three. The study guide lists eleven national holidays, among them New Year's Day, Memorial Day, Juneteenth, Independence Day, Labor Day, Veterans Day, Thanksgiving and Christmas. (Study guide, chapter 12.)

question: What is Memorial Day?
correct_answers: A holiday to honor soldiers who died in military service
explanation: Memorial Day, the last Monday in May, honors the men and women who died in service to the United States. It was first called Decoration Day, from the custom of decorating graves. (Study guide, chapter 12.)

source.title: 128 Civics Questions and Answers (2025 version)
source.quote_under_25_words: A holiday to honor soldiers who died in military service

question: What is Veterans Day?
correct_answers: A holiday to honor people in the (U.S.) military
A holiday to honor people who have served (in the U.S. military)
explanation: Veterans Day, on November 11, honors everyone who has served in the U.S. Armed Forces. It began as Armistice Day, marking the end of World War I on November 11, 1918. (Study guide, chapter 12.)

source.title: 128 Civics Questions and Answers (2025 version)
